analysis.one_liner: Holds police accountable for misconduct, limits qualified immunity, and restricts chokeholds, no-knock warrants, and racial profiling.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 220-212 in March 2021, but the Senate never voted on it and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it easier to sue and prosecute police officers who injure or kill people, including by limiting the qualified immunity defense that often shields officers from civil suits. It would ban federal no-knock warrants in drug cases, pressure states to ban chokeholds by tying federal grant money to compliance, create a national public registry of police misconduct records, and require police to collect and report data on stops, searches, and use of force, with the goal of catching racial profiling. It passed the House on a mostly party-line vote but never received a vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: People who experience police misconduct, their families, and communities disproportionately affected by use of force and racial profiling. Victims could sue officers without the qualified immunity shield, federal prosecutors could bring cases under a lower intent standard, and the public could search a national registry of officer misconduct records. Local departments would also gain access to federal grants for body cameras, training, and accreditation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of police misconduct and their families

how_it_helps.text: Lowers the criminal intent standard for convicting an officer in federal prosecutions from 'willful' to 'knowing or reckless', making federal civil-rights prosecutions easier to win.

Ends qualified immunity as a defense for local and federal officers sued for violating someone's constitutional rights, so victims can recover damages even when the exact right was not previously 'clearly established' in the courts.
Bans federal no-knock warrants in drug cases and cuts federal grant money to states that allow no-knock warrants, chokeholds, or carotid holds.

Creates a public National Police Misconduct Registry of complaints, discipline, and termination records, searchable by the public, and requires states receiving federal funds to report use-of-force data, including deaths in custody.

Bans racial profiling as a matter of federal law and requires federal, state, and local agencies receiving grants to adopt anti-profiling policies and collect stop and search data by race and ethnicity.
Authorizes roughly $1 billion in grants to support independent investigations of deadly force, civilian review boards, officer training, and accreditation of police departments.

analysis.who_pays: Police unions and officers bear the main cost: easier civil suits and federal prosecutions, a public record of misconduct, and loss of the qualified immunity shield. Local governments face more litigation and settlement costs and must meet new conditions on federal grant money. Federal taxpayers fund the new programs and registries.
analysis.who_pays_short: Police unions, officers, and local governments

drawbacks.text: Lowering the intent standard to 'knowing or reckless' means an officer could face federal prosecution for a serious error in judgment, not just deliberate wrongdoing — the objection Republicans in Congress raised against the bill.

Removing qualified immunity would increase lawsuits against officers and municipalities, raising insurance and settlement costs that local taxpayers ultimately bear, and critics argue it could make officers hesitant to act in fast-moving situations.

The bill ties federal police grant money to compliance with its training, reporting, and chokehold conditions, so states that decline could lose existing public-safety funding — a coercive federalism concern even for supporters of the goals.

The registry and use-of-force reporting requirements create significant new administrative burdens, especially for small departments, and authorizations in the bill total well over $1 billion in new federal spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — giving victims of police violence a real path to justice and creating national visibility into officer misconduct — is substantial and addresses a documented accountability gap. The main honest costs are higher litigation exposure for local governments and the risk that a 'reckless' standard reaches honest judgment errors. Weighing them, the accountability gains likely outweigh the costs, but the federalism lever of conditioning grant money and the administrative load on small departments are real design flaws worth noting.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it, but the Senate never brought it up for a vote, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 24, 2021 by Rep. Karen Bass and referred to the House Judiciary, Armed Services, and Energy and Commerce Committees.
The House passed the bill on March 3, 2021 by a vote of 220-212, with 219 of 221 voting Democrats and 1 of 211 voting Republicans in favor.
Republicans offered a motion to recommit the bill to committee, which failed 208-219 on a party-line vote immediately before final passage.
The Senate received the bill on March 9, 2021, and no further action was taken on it before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police unions and officers came out ahead: qualified immunity stayed intact, no national misconduct registry or use-of-force restrictions took effect, and existing policing practices continued unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Karen Bass
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through House passage.

for.name: President Joe Biden
for.what_they_did: Publicly urged Congress to pass the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act and issued an executive order on policing reform after the bill stalled.

for.name: Civil rights organizations including the NAACP and ACLU
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for the bill's passage after George Floyd's 2020 killing; the bill's text names such community-based organizations as intended grant partners.

against.name: 210 of 211 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage and unanimously supported the failed motion to recommit the bill to committee.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate vote; it sat after arriving in the Senate in March 2021 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the bill's elimination of qualified immunity, depriving Democrats of the votes needed to move it.

against.name: Sen. Tim Scott
against.what_they_did: Opposed the House bill and led Republican counterproposals; bipartisan talks with Rep. Bass collapsed in 2021.

against.name: Police unions, including the Fraternal Order of Police
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against limiting qualified immunity and the misconduct registry provisions.

sides.party_line_note: House passage was nearly all-Democratic: 219 of 221 voting Democrats and 1 of 211 voting Republicans voted yes, and the Senate, where Republicans held 50 of 100 seats and Democrats 50, never voted at all.

industries.industry: Police labor unions and law enforcement officers
industries.note: The bill removes qualified immunity as a shield in civil suits, lowers the criminal intent standard for federal prosecution, and creates a public registry of officer misconduct — directly reducing protections officers and their unions currently enjoy. Their interest in preserving those protections runs against accountability for the public.

Departments would gain federal grant money for body cameras, training, and accreditation, but would face new liabilities, mandatory data reporting, and conditions on existing grant funds, including possible funding cuts for noncompliance.

The bill requires 5% of grant funds to go toward accreditation and directs the Justice Department to partner with accreditation organizations and set uniform national standards through them, locking in their role as the channel for police oversight standards. Their business grows alongside the public's interest in professionalized policing.

industries.industry: Body camera and policing technology manufacturers
industries.note: The bill mandates body cameras and in-car recording for federal officers and funds camera programs for local departments, creating a large new customer base. The mandate serves the public's interest in recorded encounters while guaranteeing the industry revenue.
